title: Curiosity Killer
excerpt: How do kids stay curious about so many things, and what happens to us that we stop asking questions?
content:
I love bike rides. They make me feel more alive, so much so that every week I travel at least 4-5 times by bike. I don't know how to ride a motorcycle myself, so I just book an Uber Bike, and honestly it's better than riding and making all the decisions yourself. Here you can just sit back, enjoy, observe, and feel the wind flowing through your hair.

A few days ago, coming back home from a day out with my friends, I booked an Uber bike. When the driver arrived and handed me the helmet, he looked at me from top to bottom, called me a hippie, and laughed it off.

Since I've grown my hair long and started dressing in a way that interests me, not to appease someone else, and because of that I get a lot of stares whenever I go out in public, a lot of them judgemental. When this person called me a hippie I did feel defensive, but the main thing that came to my mind was why dressing differently seems to be something people make fun of. Maybe it's because we've been trained since childhood to see DIFFERENT = BAD.

I've started doing this thing where I notice one thing daily and try to dig deep into it. I even made an "OBSERVATIONS" section on my website where I post these. So today, thinking about what my topic could be, it hit me that during childhood I used to be so curious I never had to ask myself what I should observe. How are kids so curious about so many things, and what happens to us that we stop observing, stop asking questions?

Kids are born curious because the world is new to them, and they're not familiar with quite literally anything. As they develop their senses and their thinking, they question everything, observing closely whatever interests them, whatever feels new, whatever is fascinating.

So why, when those same kids grow up, is there no curiosity left, as if it was never there to begin with? A few things decide that. Is the kid even allowed to be curious? Is the kid in an environment that supports that curiosity, one it can actually thrive in? Is the kid secure around the people in that environment?

At home we're comfortable around our parents, and as kids we don't rethink before doing something, we just experiment, observe, ask questions. But the moment a child is enrolled in school, that safety of play gets snatched away. Now the child is expected to perform in a specific manner, to learn exactly what he's taught, with no room left for questions that are so-called "out of syllabus." And so the kid stops asking.

Those same kids, once their curiosity has been taken from them, grow up to see anyone still asking questions, still doing things differently, still going out of syllabus, as a bad example. If a kid is scribbling on a clean sheet of paper, that's bad. And when those grown kids see someone dressing differently, they don't stop for a moment to wonder why. They show no curiosity, only judgment. It isn't really their fault, it's what society trained them to become, and so they go on to raise another generation of curiosity killers.

Not people like me, though. At this stage I've gotten stubborn about the way I want to experiment, the way I want to explore. But to a small kid, a curiosity killer is one of the worst things that can happen to them. And this is where I find myself wishing I could go back to that Uber driver's childhood, appreciate him for scribbling badly on a page, and hand him a canvas and paint instead, just to let that curiosity thrive.

I wish...

title: Why I Built LoreGraph
excerpt: Building a place to organize ideas. Graph databases, React Flow, and why relationships matter more than notes.
content:
Most note-taking apps treat thoughts as isolated files in nested folders. But the human mind doesn't think in folders—it thinks in associative graphs.

When I was writing lore for a game world, I kept running into the same frustration: character A met character B at location C during event D. If I put that in a folder called 'Characters', the geographical context was lost. If I filed it under 'Locations', the timeline disappeared.

So I built LoreGraph.

LoreGraph is a visual node-based workspace where entities and relationships are first-class citizens. You draw connections between concepts, assign semantic edges ('betrayed by', 'ancestor of', 'discovered at'), and let the graph reveal patterns you didn't even know existed.

Here are three big lessons I learned while building it:

1. Canvas performance is hard. Rendering hundreds of SVG nodes with live Bezier curves forces you to get comfortable with spatial indexing (quadtrees) and viewport culling.
2. Less UI is more canvas. Every toolbar button you add steals mental space from the graph.
3. The structure of your notes influences the structure of your thoughts. Once you start linking concepts explicitly, your thinking becomes noticeably clearer.

title: Why I keep rebuilding my portfolio
excerpt: Every new portfolio is a new idea of who I am. This one might actually stick.
content:
I have rebuilt my personal website at least six times in the last three years. Every single time, I convince myself: 'This is the final design. This is timeless.'

And two months later, I stare at it and cringe.

For a long time I felt guilty about this. Friends would ask, 'Why are you redesigning again? Just ship something and leave it.' It felt like procrastination masked as productive work.

Then I realized what a personal website actually is: it isn't a resume, and it isn't an corporate landing page. It's a digital greenhouse. You prune it, you re-pot things, you see what sprouted and what died.

This current version—with its soft paper tones, dark inked borders, and handwritten notes—feels closer to my actual desk than anything I've built before. It's imperfect on purpose. And that's why I think it might finally stay.

title: Games are strange teachers
excerpt: Games taught me more about systems thinking than most college courses ever did.
content:
When you play a strategy or simulation game, you aren't just pushing buttons. You are calibrating a mental model of an invisible dynamic system.

In Factorio, you learn about bottlenecks and asynchronous queues. In Civilization, you learn about opportunity cost and delayed gratification. In chess, you learn how minor tactical gains mean nothing if your overarching position is compromised.

Formal education often presents knowledge in static, linear chapters. Games present knowledge as feedback loops: you take an action, the state changes, the environment pushes back, and you adjust your thesis.

If we designed software tools with the same feedback density as good video games, work wouldn't feel like a chore—it would feel like exploration.

title: Things books make me notice
excerpt: Reading fiction has made me a better observer and a calmer debugger.
content:
Someone once asked me why a software builder reads so much fiction instead of technical textbooks or business guides.

Here is my answer: technical books teach you syntax; fiction teaches you how humans construct meaning.

When Samantha Harvey describes sixteen orbital sunrises a day in 'Orbital', she isn't giving you an astronomy lecture. She is giving you a lens to look at the fragile speck of dirt we call home. When Adrian Tchaikovsky writes from the perspective of an uplifted spider civilization in 'Children of Time', he forces your mind to abandon human-centric assumptions.

That mental elasticity translates directly into engineering. When a distributed system behaves erratically at 2 AM, the bug rarely lives in what you already understand. It lives in the assumptions you forgot you were making.

title: On starting things I never finish
excerpt: Half the folders in my projects directory are abandoned. I've made peace with that.
content:
My hard drive is a graveyard of half-baked prototypes, three-page short stories, and games with only one functioning jump animation.

For years I considered this a personal flaw. Society fetishizes 'finishing.' Books tell you to execute to completion or not bother starting.

But creative exploration doesn't work on linear schedules. A prototype isn't a failure just because it didn't become a venture-backed SaaS. Often, the single insight you gained while failing to finish project A is the exact building block that makes project B possible.

Start things without demanding that they justify their existence. Some seeds are meant to become giant oaks; others are just meant to fertilize the soil.

title: Limited circle of warmth
excerpt: You only have enough emotional energy to keep a few people and ideas truly warm.
content:
There is an old campfire metaphor I keep coming back to: a small fire cannot warm the entire forest. If you try to spread the embers too thin, the fire goes out and everyone freezes.

In the internet age, we are encouraged to care about everything simultaneously. Every piece of news, every stranger's critique, every trending outrage demands emotional bandwidth.

Drawing your circle smaller isn't apathy. It's stewardship. You decide who and what sits inside the warmth of your attention, and you protect that perimeter fiercely.

title: Simple Stupid
excerpt: Clever code is a liability. Boring code is a superpower.
content:
The hallmark of junior engineering is writing code that shows how smart you are. The hallmark of seasoned engineering is writing code so simple that any tired human can read it at 3 AM.

Whenever I'm tempted to introduce an elaborate abstraction, a custom caching layer, or an exotic design pattern, I force myself to ask:

'Could this just be a plain function?'
'Could this just be a straightforward loop?'

Nine times out of ten, the answer is yes. Complexity is an insidious tax you pay every single day. Keep it simple. Keep it boring. Keep it working.

title: Mind Roams
excerpt: What happens when you walk without headphones, without podcasts, without an agenda.
content:
Almost nobody walks in silence anymore. We queue up podcasts at 1.5x speed, shuffle playlists, or call someone the second our shoes hit the pavement.

Last month I started taking 45-minute daily walks with literally nothing in my ears. The first ten minutes are unbearable—your brain screams for dopamine stimulation.

And then something magical happens: the ambient static fades, and your subconscious mind finally gets a turn to speak. The bugs you were stuck on unravel themselves. The sentences you couldn't phrase fall into place. Boredom is not the enemy of creativity; it is its birth chamber.

title: Websites I Love
excerpt: A curated tribute to personal corners of the web that feel like living rooms, not storefronts.
content:
The modern commercial web is homogenized. Everything uses the same geometric sans-serif, the same rounded button gradients, and the same cookie-cutter hero banner.

But in the quiet corners of the indie web, people are still making weird, wonderful things. Sites shaped like notebooks. Sites shaped like 90s OS desktops. Sites with hand-drawn navigation maps and personal guestbooks.

This website is my contribution to that lineage. Not a startup landing page designed to optimize conversion metrics, but a cozy digital cabinet where you can pull out drawers and poke around.

title: Art for Artist
excerpt: Why making bad drawings with zero commercial value keeps the creative soul alive.
content:
If you monetize everything you enjoy, you end up enjoying nothing.

I draw with markers and cheap ink pens almost every evening. None of it is sold, none of it is on Behance, and most of it wouldn't pass a basic art school critique. And that is precisely why it is sacred to me.

When there are no clients, no algorithms, and no performance indicators, the act of creation returns to pure play. You scribble because the friction of ink on paper feels good. That is enough.

title: Learn How to Learn
excerpt: Frameworks for absorbing new domains from scratch without getting overwhelmed.
content:
Every time I pick up a new discipline—whether it's learning Rust, studying chess endgames, or understanding graph databases—I follow a simple four-stage protocol:

1. Immersion without understanding: Skim top books and repositories for a weekend just to absorb the vocabulary.
2. Build the smallest broken thing: Don't read tutorials for months. Build a 50-line toy script that immediately breaks.
3. Identify the missing primitive: Debugging that failure reveals the core concept you actually need to learn.
4. Teach it to an imaginary ten-year-old: If you can't explain it without using the domain's jargon, you don't understand it yet.

Meta-learning is the highest-leverage skill in the world.
